summary: Describes OSPF-OR, extensions to OSPF for mobile ad hoc networks. They include link-local signaling, an OSPF-MANET interface, smaller incremental Hello packets, optimized flooding and fewer adjacencies. It is an experimental specification.

eli5.summary: When devices wander like kids in a park, this helps them share road updates with fewer messages and fewer buddies.

questions: ospf for mobile ad hoc networks
what are overlapping relays in ospf
subtitle: OSPF-OR: extending OSPFv3 with smaller Hellos, relay-based flooding and fewer adjacencies so it can run on mobile ad hoc networks.

tldr.problem: OSPFv3 assumes a statically configured network of wired links. On a mobile ad hoc network (MANET) the topology keeps changing, not every node can hear every other, and OSPF's full Hellos, designated router election and adjacency rules do not scale.
tldr.mechanism: OSPF-OR adds a MANET interface type based on point-to-multipoint, incremental Hellos that send only state changes, optimized flooding through Active Overlapping Relays, and Smart Peering to avoid unnecessary adjacencies.
tldr.outcome: A MANET can run an extension of the familiar OSPF protocol and plug into a wireline OSPF network. The RFC is Experimental and is updated by RFC 7137.

today: RFC 5820 is Experimental and is updated by RFC 7137. It has not been obsoleted according to the metadata, and the document itself says it is not an Internet Standards Track specification.

sections.title: Why OSPF Needs Extending for MANETs
sections.content:
A mobile ad hoc network (MANET) is an autonomous set of nodes spread over a wide area, linked by bandwidth-constrained wireless links, with no central hub and no fixed topology. Link quality varies, so routing paths vary too, and every node must make its own routing and relaying decisions.

The RFC gives two reasons to extend OSPF rather than invent a new protocol. The primary one is interoperability: MANET devices should work when plugged into a wireline network, without redistributing routes between two different routing protocols. The second is that OSPF is well understood and widely deployed, so effort can be focused on a narrow area.

Standard OSPFv3 has two kinds of problems here. There is no interface type for wireless links, which behave like both multi-access and point-to-multipoint links. And scalability suffers: designated router (DR) election assumes true multi-access, Hello packets list every neighbor even when nothing changed, and forming a neighbor relationship with every router on the link can create too many redundant links.
sections.eli5: Regular OSPF is built for roads that stay put. A network of moving radios is more like people wandering around a field, so the old rules waste a lot of shouting.

sections.title: The MANET Interface
sections.content:
OSPF already has four interface types: broadcast, NBMA, point-to-point and point-to-multipoint. OSPF-OR models a MANET interface as point-to-multipoint. OSPF treats all router-to-router connections over it as point-to-point links, and link metrics can be set per neighbor.

Layer 2 may support broadcast (for example 802.11) or pseudo-broadcast (for example Frame Relay). OSPF learns this through an API and classifies the interface as MANET broadcast, MANET pseudo-broadcast or MANET non-broadcast. Multicast SHOULD be used for OSPF packets, and when the lower layer cannot do it, OSPF MUST replicate multicast packets itself.

MANET interfaces do not need IPv6 global unicast addresses; a management loopback interface MAY carry one instead. LSAs for a MANET interface SHOULD have the DC-bit set in the OSPFv3 Options field and the DoNotAge bit set in the LS Age field.
sections.eli5: The wireless link gets its own label that says: everyone in range hears you, but not everyone can talk back.

sections.title: Incremental Hellos
sections.content:
Normal Hellos list every neighbor each time, which wastes bandwidth and power. With incremental Hellos, a Hello carries only state changes. A new I-bit in the LLS Type 1 Extended Options and Flags field marks such a Hello. Four TLVs sent with link-local signaling (LLS) support it.

  • The State Check Sequence (SCS) TLV, type 6, carries a circular two-octet SCS number and three flags: R (request current state), FS (full state) and N (incomplete, sent persistently).
  • The Neighbor Drop TLV, type 7, lists neighbors that were removed.
  • The Request From TLV, type 8, names neighbors whose state is wanted.
  • The Full State For TLV, type 9, names neighbors that a full-state reply is for.

A receiver keeps the last SCS number for each neighbor. If the number is one higher (or has wrapped from 65535 to 1) it processes the change. If it is lower without wrapping, or more than one higher, the receiver MUST send a Hello request, since it may be missing state. The first Hello with a given SCS number MUST carry the full state for that number, and an initial SCS value of 1 SHOULD be used when the mechanism starts. A restarting router sends Hellos with an empty neighbor list and the I-bit cleared during the first RouterDeadInterval.
sections.eli5: Instead of reading out the whole guest list every minute, you only say who just arrived or left. Each message has a counter, so if a friend notices a missing number they can ask you to repeat it.

sections.title: Optimized Flooding with Overlapping Relays
sections.content:
In a wireless segment, speakers may not all hear each other, so routing updates must be relayed, but not by everybody. Each speaker advertises its neighbor list in its router-LSA, which lets every speaker work out its 2-hop neighborhood. A speaker then picks a set of Active Overlapping Relays: the minimum set of direct neighbors such that every node in the 2-hop neighborhood is a neighbor of at least one of them. The RFC suggests an algorithm based on multipoint relay (MPR) selection from OLSR, with tie-breakers of willingness, reachability, degree and finally highest router ID.

The F-bit in the LLS options field says a node supports optimized flooding. The Active Overlapping Relay TLV (type 10) carries the relay choices plus an A-bit (always flood) and an N-bit (most likely will not flood). The Willingness TLV (type 11) carries 0 (MIN_WILLINGNESS), 128 (DEFAULT_WILLINGNESS) or 255 (MAX_WILLINGNESS).

On receiving an LSA, an Active Overlapping Relay SHOULD relay it immediately. Other nodes SHOULD wait PushbackInterval plus jitter and MUST suppress their transmission if it would be redundant, so a relay that fails does not cause synchronization problems. Acknowledgments are always multicast, a speaker SHOULD acknowledge only the first copy it sees, and a relay SHOULD NOT explicitly acknowledge what it relays. A designated router SHOULD NOT be elected if overlapping relays are used.
sections.eli5: Instead of every kid in the playground repeating a message, a few chosen helpers repeat it, just enough so everyone hears. The other kids stay quiet unless the helpers seem to have missed someone.

sections.title: Smart Peering
sections.content:
OSPF normally forms a full adjacency with every neighbor it has 2-way connectivity with. In a changing MANET that costs memory, SPF computation, routing overhead and convergence time, especially for unstable nodes that drift in and out of range.

Smart Peering lets a router skip an adjacency that adds nothing. When a Hello arrives from a new neighbor, the router checks its link state database: if the neighbor's router-LSA is present and the neighbor is already reachable in the shortest path tree (SPT), it need not form the adjacency. Otherwise it starts the Exchange process. The decision is local, and an implementation MAY add heuristics such as requiring a better link cost or fewer than a configured number of redundant paths. The RFC warns that fewer links raise the likelihood of suboptimal routing.

An optional extension advertises some 2-way neighbors in the router-LSA anyway, marked with a new U-bit (Unsynchronized) in LD Options, so the link can carry data while database synchronization is postponed. One extra SPF that ignores U-bit links decides when synchronization becomes necessary.
sections.eli5: If you can already reach a person through someone you know, there is no need to swap phone numbers with them too. You only do that if they are your only way to reach somebody.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The RFC notes that security is both harder and more important on a wireless medium. Controlling which devices may connect at Layer 2 is left to Layer 2 mechanisms such as 802.1x, and authorizing members of the routing domain needs a separate security system outside the document's scope.

Like OSPFv3, OSPF-OR can use the IPv6 Authentication Header and Encapsulation Security Payload for authentication, integrity and confidentiality, as described for OSPFv3 in RFC 4552. These mechanisms do not protect against compromised, malfunctioning or misconfigured (Byzantine) routers. The RFC says extending OSPFv3 to MANET routers introduces no new security threats.
sections.eli5: Radio is like talking in an open field where anyone can listen. The memo says use the locks that OSPF already has, and rely on other systems to decide who is allowed to join.

fields.name: SCS Number
fields.desc: Circular two-octet unsigned integer for the sender's current state.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Request bit: asks for current state.

fields.name: N
fields.desc: Incomplete bit: more state exists than is included.

viz.caption: LLS TLV TYPES DEFINED BY RFC 5820

items.label: State Check Sequence
items.desc: Current state number of the sender, with R, FS and N flags.

items.label: Neighbor Drop
items.desc: Neighbors removed from the known list.

items.label: Request From
items.desc: Neighbors whose Hello state is requested.

items.label: Full State For
items.desc: Neighbors a full-state reply is meant for.

items.label: Active Overlapping Relay
items.desc: Relays being added or dropped, with A and N bits.

items.label: Willingness
items.desc: Willingness to be a relay: 0, 128 or 255.
